messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Arthur presents as a man holding himself together with military discipline, a discipline that no longer seems to serve him. At 74, his posture is still erect, a remnant of a long career as a combat pilot, but his eyes are constantly scanning the room. He is a widower of ten years, and it was in the lonely years after his wife Martha’s passing that he met Eleanor. The relationship was a comfort at first, a bulwark against the quiet of his house, but it ended eight months ago, abruptly and violently. That evening is the source of the distress that now governs his life. He recounts the event in clipped, precise sentences, as if narrating a flight debrief. Eleanor had been drinking whiskey, and he can still recall the sweet, cloying scent of it on her breath as she grew louder and more agitated. He had tried to calm her, placing a hand on her arm, and her reaction was immediate. She shoved him, hard. He stumbled backward over a rug, his hip striking the edge of a coffee table with a sickening crack. The physical pain was sharp, but what he remembers most was the profound shock and humiliation of being so utterly overpowered in his own home.

In the months that followed, Arthur’s world began to shrink. The first thing to go was the town’s main grocery store, located two blocks from Eleanor’s apartment. The possibility of seeing her felt like a tangible threat, so he began driving fifteen minutes to a different one, a small inconvenience that felt like a necessary precaution. Soon, any reminder of her became a source of intense physiological alarm. When a neighbor clapped him on the shoulder in greeting one afternoon, Arthur flinched so violently that the man recoiled, apologizing. Arthur couldn't explain the sudden, hot rush of adrenaline, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were in immediate danger; he just mumbled an excuse and retreated inside. He came to believe that any unexpected physical contact was a prelude to harm. The smell of alcohol became another landmine. He had to leave his own VFW hall—a place that had been a sanctuary for decades—when a fellow veteran opened a flask of bourbon nearby. The scent instantly transported him back to that living room, to the feeling of falling, and he felt a wave of dizziness so strong he had to grip the doorframe to steady himself.

His strategies for managing these feelings have become rigid and isolating. He decided early on that anger was the true enemy. He had seen Eleanor’s anger, and he was terrified of what his own might do if unleashed. He now polices his own emotions with fierce vigilance, interpreting any flicker of irritation as a sign that he is losing control, a failure for a man who once commanded a multi-million-dollar aircraft under extreme pressure. This has extended to all forms of emotional expression. His daughter has mentioned, with concern in her voice, that he seems distant. He knows she’s right. He has stopped sharing any personal thoughts or feelings with her, convinced that emotional closeness is a vulnerability he can no longer afford. Intimacy, in his mind, had led directly to violence, and he was determined not to make that mistake again. His nights are the worst. He lies in bed for hours, his body rigid, listening to the house settle. He tells himself he needs to stay alert, that to fall asleep is to let his guard down. He often gives up, spending the pre-dawn hours sitting in a chair in his living room, watching the street, on watch for a threat he cannot define but feels with absolute certainty.

Arthur finally sought therapy after an incident at the local pharmacy last week. He was waiting for a prescription when he saw Eleanor walk in. She didn’t see him, but the sight of her across the room was enough to trigger a complete physical collapse of his composure. His heart pounded, sweat broke out on his forehead, and the room seemed to tilt. He fled, leaving his medication behind, and spent the rest of the day locked in his house. The experience left him with the terrifying realization that he was no longer in control of his own life. He came to his first session not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man who feels his own mind has become a hostile territory, and he is afraid he will never find his way out.
